title: Resolving the heart of the Wolf-Rayet binary Apep with ALMA
comment: 6 pages, 3 figures, accepted for publication in A&A
summary: The Wolf-Rayet (WR) phase is a critical stage in the evolution of massive stars. During this phase, the stars experience a large mass loss in the form of fast winds that are enriched with heavy elements. There are only a few WR binaries in the galaxy, with Apep being a truly exceptional system exhibiting a bright colliding-wind region at radio wavelengths and an impressive dust plume in the infrared. Although the angular separation between the two (WN and WC) components has been indirectly inferred to be about 47 mas, it has yet to be confirmed through direct measurements. We aim to image the Apep system at millimetre wavelengths to determine the position of the WR stars and their mass-loss rates. We observed Apep with ALMA in Bands 6 and 7 in a large baseline configuration, achieving an angular resolution of approximately 20 mas. We used a canonical spherical wind model to convert the measured flux densities into wind mass-loss rates. Towards Apep, we detect point-like emission coming from the WN star and elongated emission most likely from the colliding-wind region; the WC star is not detected. We also detect the O star at 0.7'' that has been associated with the system. Our analysis favours mass-loss rates for the WN and WC components of $\dot{M}_\mathrm{WN}\sim 2\times10^{-5}\,M_\odot \,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$ and $\dot{M}_\mathrm{WC}\sim10^{-5}\,M_\odot\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$, respectively. The mass-loss rates of the WR stars are significantly lower than previously reported, and we examine several factors that may account for this discrepancy. The diffuse emission from the colliding-wind region cannot be accounted for by the synchrotron flux, and thus additional free-free or dust emission is present.

AI.tldr: ALMA Band 6/7 imaging of the exceptional WR binary Apep at ~20 mas resolution detects point-like emission from the WN star and extended colliding-wind emission, but no WC star; derived mass-loss rates are significantly lower than previously reported.
AI.motivation: Apep is a rare, exceptional Galactic Wolf-Rayet binary with a bright radio colliding-wind region and an infrared dust plume. Its component separation (~47 mas) was only indirectly inferred and never directly confirmed, and the mass-loss rates of its WN and WC stars remain uncertain.
AI.method: Millimetre observations with ALMA in Bands 6 and 7 using a large baseline configuration, reaching ~20 mas angular resolution. A canonical spherical wind model was used to convert measured flux densities into wind mass-loss rates.
AI.result: Point-like emission is detected from the WN star plus elongated emission likely from the colliding-wind region; the WC star is undetected, and the associated O star is detected at 0.7''. Mass-loss rates are derived as Mdot_WN ~ 2e-5 Msun/yr and Mdot_WC ~ 1e-5 Msun/yr, significantly lower than earlier values. The diffuse colliding-wind emission exceeds the expected synchrotron flux, implying additional free-free or dust emission.
AI.conclusion: The Apep system is spatially resolved at mm wavelengths, directly constraining component positions and yielding revised, lower mass-loss rates. The excess diffuse emission indicates free-free and/or dust contributions beyond synchrotron in the colliding-wind region.

title: Discovery of eclipses in the cataclysmic variable MASTER OT J232100.42+494614.0
comment: 11 pages, 8 figures
summary: I performed photometric observations of the poorly studied cataclysmic variable MASTER OT J232100.42+494614.0 and discovered eclipses. I observed nine eclipses over two groups of closely spaced nights, separated by a 12-month interval. I precisely calculated the orbital period of the system to be Porb=0.212371533+\-0.000000069 days. For the eclipses, I created an ephemeris that is accurate for a long time span and suitable for analysing changes in the orbital period. The star's brightness outside of the eclipses varied between 15.61+\-0.02 and 18.04+\-0.05 mag. As the brightness decreased, the eclipses became more profound whereas its width remained unchanged. The average depth of eclipses was 1.36+\-0.03 mag, and the average width at half-depth was 0.0512(15) phases. I calculated the possible inclination of the orbit to be between 72.8 and 76.3 degrees, and the range of the average absolute V-band magnitude of the disc to be between 6.37+\-0.35 and 6.68+\-0.35 mag. Although the light curve of MASTER OT J232100.42+494614.0 from the ZTF survey showed insufficiently large outbursts with amplitudes less than 2.5 mag, it should be classified as a dwarf nova, as the average disc brightness and mass transfer rate are below the threshold for thermal instability.

AI.tldr: Photometric monitoring of MASTER OT J232100.42+494614.0 revealed eclipses, yielding a precise orbital period (0.212371533 d), an eclipse ephemeris, and constraints on inclination and disc brightness; the object is classified as a dwarf nova despite weak ZTF outbursts.
AI.motivation: The system MASTER OT J232100.42+494614.0 is poorly studied, and its nature and orbital parameters were largely unknown, motivating dedicated photometric characterization.
AI.method: Time-resolved photometry over two groups of nights separated by 12 months, capturing nine eclipses; determination of orbital period, construction of a long-baseline ephemeris, and measurement of eclipse depth, width, out-of-eclipse brightness, inclination, and absolute V-band disc magnitude; comparison with ZTF survey light curve.
AI.result: Orbital period Porb = 0.212371533 ± 0.000000069 d. Out-of-eclipse brightness ranged 15.61 ± 0.02 to 18.04 ± 0.05 mag; eclipses deepened as brightness declined while width stayed constant. Mean eclipse depth 1.36 ± 0.03 mag; mean half-depth width 0.0512(15) phases. Inclination 72.8–76.3°; mean absolute V-band disc magnitude 6.37 ± 0.35 to 6.68 ± 0.35 mag. ZTF outbursts have amplitudes < 2.5 mag.
AI.conclusion: The object is an eclipsing cataclysmic variable classified as a dwarf nova, since its average disc brightness and mass-transfer rate fall below the thermal instability threshold, notwithstanding its relatively weak outbursts.

title: Let Sleeping Stars Li: Mapping Turnoff Lithium, the Lithium Dip, & Testing Standard Model Predictions in GALAH DR4 Subgiants
comment: 37 Pages; 15 Figures; Submitted to ApJ; Data available upon request (smedile.1@osu.edu); comments welcome
summary: Lithium is an excellent tracer of stellar mixing. We reconstruct the end of the main sequence lithium depletion pattern using the GALAH DR4 3D-NLTE lithium dataset for 22,442 stars, complemented by masses and subgiant lithium dilution factors inferred from YREC stellar models. We recover the two canonical features seen in clusters: a cool plateau ($\mathrm{M_{[Fe/H]_{\odot}}} \sim 1.2 \mathrm{M_\odot}$) with a median $A(Li) = 2.42$, and a steep plunge into the lithium dip ($\mathrm{M_{[Fe/H]_{\odot}}} \sim 1.35 \mathrm{M_\odot}$) dominated by upper limits at $A(Li) < 1.5$. Above the dip, our data reveal a striking new pattern with a wide range of abundances. We argue this reflects severe rotationally induced mixing in most stars, with lithium preserved in a minority where gravitational settling suppresses mixing. Lithium depletion with intrinsic dispersion is universal across the sample. Predicted and observed dilution trends agree well below the dip. For higher-mass stars, dilution corrections agree with standard models, but our upper envelope lies below open cluster values. We attribute this to a shallower lithium preservation zone and further evidence for gravitational settling and radiative levitation. We detect lithium in $\approx25\%$ of dip stars, whereas clusters show none; neither blurring of a narrow mass feature nor binary contamination fully explains this. The cool plateau is 0.8 dex below the solar meteoritic value across a wide range of $[Fe/H]$. After accounting for pre-main sequence depletion, the plateau is elevated at $\geq [Fe/H]_{\odot}$, possibly evidence for lithium production.

AI.tldr: Using GALAH DR4 3D-NLTE lithium abundances for 22,442 stars, this work reconstructs the terminal main-sequence lithium depletion pattern and finds canonical plateau and dip features plus a new wide-abundance regime above the dip, interpreted as rotationally induced mixing modulated by gravitational settling.
AI.motivation: Lithium is an excellent tracer of stellar mixing, and a large, homogeneous sample allows reconstruction of the end-of-main-sequence lithium depletion pattern and its intrinsic dispersion, testing mixing, settling, and levitation physics against cluster benchmarks.
AI.method: Reconstructs the terminal main-sequence lithium depletion pattern from GALAH DR4 3D-NLTE lithium abundances for 22,442 stars, with masses and subgiant lithium dilution factors derived from YREC stellar models, and compares dilution trends and upper/lower envelopes to open-cluster values.
AI.result: Recovers the cool plateau (M ~ 1.2 Msun, median A(Li) = 2.42) and the steep lithium dip (M ~ 1.35 Msun, upper limits A(Li) < 1.5). Above the dip, a striking wide spread in abundances appears, attributed to severe rotationally induced mixing with lithium preserved in a minority where gravitational settling suppresses mixing. Lithium depletion with intrinsic dispersion is universal; predicted and observed dilution agree below the dip; for higher masses the upper envelope lies below open-cluster values. Lithium is detected in ~25% of dip stars versus none in clusters. The plateau sits 0.8 dex below the meteoritic value across a wide [Fe/H] range and is elevated at >= solar metallicity after pre-main-sequence correction.
AI.conclusion: The data support universal lithium depletion with intrinsic scatter, rotationally induced mixing as the dominant driver above the dip, and an important role for gravitational settling and radiative levitation (a shallower lithium preservation zone at higher masses). Unexplained dip-star lithium (~25%) challenges simple feature-blurring or binary explanations, and the elevated plateau at >= solar [Fe/H] may hint at lithium production.

title: Searching for Dwarf Novae in 47 Tucanae
summary: The globular cluster 47 Tucanae has 43 strong cataclysmic variable candidates, four of which are confirmed dwarf novae. Tidal capture theory predicts the existence of dozens of dwarf novae, suggesting more are undiscovered. Using 435 nm and 475 nm long exposure images from Hubble's ACS camera, we searched five epochs of archival Hubble images and did not find any variability at the scale of a dwarf nova eruption. We found 1 previously undiscovered variable object on the main sequence that could not be classified as a CV; the object experienced a change of approximately 0.3 Mag in 425 nm, and 0.2 mag in 635 nm over the course of 12 days. The lack of new CV detections in 47 Tucanae could be a result of the short timescale of the DN eruption, and a low observing probability. However, this null result may also support research suggesting most CVs in globular clusters are not dynamically formed, and tidal capture theory overestimates the detectable CV population.

AI.tldr: A search of archival Hubble ACS images of 47 Tucanae found no new dwarf nova eruptions, but one unclassified main-sequence variable; the null result hints that most cluster CVs are not dynamically formed and that tidal capture theory overestimates the detectable CV population.
AI.motivation: 47 Tucanae hosts 43 strong CV candidates, only four confirmed dwarf novae, and tidal capture theory predicts dozens of dwarf novae, implying many remain undiscovered. The authors test whether additional dwarf novae can be found via variability.
AI.method: Analysis of five epochs of archival Hubble ACS long-exposure images in 435 nm and 475 nm bands, searching for variability at the scale of a dwarf nova eruption.
AI.result: No dwarf nova-scale variability was detected. One previously undiscovered variable on the main sequence, not classifiable as a CV, changed by ~0.3 mag at 425 nm and ~0.2 mag at 635 nm over 12 days.
AI.conclusion: The absence of new CV detections may reflect the short duration of DN eruptions and low observing probability, but may also support the view that most globular cluster CVs are not dynamically formed and that tidal capture theory overestimates the detectable CV population.

title: Observational Signatures of Kerr Black Hole Lensing
comment: accepted to MNRAS, October 2026
summary: Gravitational lensing by rotating black holes is modeled, and the null geodesic equations in the strong field regime are integrated numerically. Observational signatures of the black hole spin parameter are identified by comparing image locations and shapes of extended sources at different a values. For the black hole at the center of our galaxy, angular resolutions of the order of hundreds of micro arc seconds are needed to distinguish between the true source position and gravitationally lensed image position. Angular resolution below one micro arc second is needed to determine the spin parameter of the galactic black hole using gravitational lensing.

AI.tldr: The paper models gravitational lensing by rotating (Kerr) black holes, numerically integrates null geodesics in the strong-field regime, and identifies observational signatures of the spin parameter a via image positions/shapes of extended sources. Distinguishing the true source position from its lensed image for the Galactic center black hole requires angular resolutions of order hundreds of microarcseconds, while determining the spin parameter via lensing requires sub-microarcsecond resolution.
AI.motivation: Gravitational lensing in the strong-field regime near rotating black holes encodes the spin parameter, but the observational requirements (angular resolution) needed to extract it have not been clearly quantified. The paper aims to assess the feasibility of using lensing signatures to probe black hole spin.
AI.method: Strong-field null geodesic equations around a rotating (Kerr) black hole are formulated and integrated numerically. Image locations and shapes of extended sources are compared across different values of the spin parameter a, and the required angular resolution is estimated for the Galactic center black hole.
AI.result: Spin-dependent differences appear in the positions and shapes of lensed images of extended sources. For the Galactic black hole, hundreds of microarcseconds of angular resolution are needed to separate the true source position from the lensed image position, whereas sub-microarcsecond resolution is required to determine the spin parameter from lensing.
AI.conclusion: Lensing by rotating black holes provides a potential probe of spin, but extracting the spin parameter demands angular resolution far beyond current capabilities (~sub-microarcsecond), making spin determination via Galactic black hole lensing observationally challenging with present instruments.

title: Double Trouble: How Unresolved Spectroscopic Binary Stars Skew GALAH DR4 Stellar Parameters
summary: Unresolved binary stars introduce systematic biases in stellar parameter estimates when analysed assuming a single star. Using $\sim$917{,}000 spectra from the Galactic Archaeology with HERMES (GALAH) Data Release 4 (DR4), we develop a binary spectral model that fits each observed spectrum as the superposition of two synthetic spectra generated from the same model architecture used by GALAH DR4. These generative spectral models take as input: effective temperature ($T_\mathrm{eff}$), surface gravity ($\log g$), iron abundance ([Fe/H]), projected rotation velocity ($v \sin i$), microturbulence velocity ($v_\mathrm{mic}$), and radial velocity ($v_\mathrm{rad}$). In our binary model, $T_\mathrm{eff}$ and $\log g$ are not fitted directly but are instead interpolated from PARSEC isochrones based on stellar mass and age, under the assumption that both components formed contemporaneously with the same compositions. We fit for the primary and secondary masses, a common age and [Fe/H], as well as individual $v \sin i$, $v_\mathrm{mic}$, and $v_\mathrm{rad}$ for each component. After iterative optimization and conservative quality cuts to ensure robust detections, we identify $\sim$12{,}911 candidate binary systems. We quantify typical biases introduced by unresolved binarity: $T_\mathrm{eff}$ shifts of $-142$ to $+200$ K, $\log g$ shifts of $-0.070$ to $+0.35$ dex, and [Fe/H] shifts of $-0.055$ to $+0.13$ dex. Despite our conservative approach reducing the number of detections, we recover known trends of increasing binary fraction with higher primary mass and lower metallicity, thus reflecting the broad trends of binary populations. Accounting for unresolved binaries is essential for accurate stellar population modelling and for interpreting spectroscopic surveys--particularly in low-metallicity systems or populations with more massive stars.

AI.tldr: A binary spectral model fit to ~917,000 GALAH DR4 spectra identifies ~12,911 unresolved binary candidates and quantifies the systematic biases that binarity introduces in T_eff, log g, and [Fe/H].
AI.motivation: Unresolved binary stars bias single-star analyses of spectroscopic surveys, so stellar parameter estimates and population modelling require a dedicated binary treatment and a quantification of the resulting offsets.
AI.method: Each GALAH DR4 spectrum is modelled as the superposition of two synthetic spectra from the same generative architecture used in DR4, parameterised by T_eff, log g, [Fe/H], v sin i, v_mic, and v_rad. T_eff and log g are not fitted directly but interpolated from PARSEC isochrones using mass and age, assuming coeval formation and shared composition. Free parameters are primary and secondary mass, common age and [Fe/H], and per-component v sin i, v_mic, and v_rad. Iterative optimisation followed by conservative quality cuts yields robust detections.
AI.result: ~12,911 candidate binary systems are identified from ~917,000 spectra. Typical unresolved-binarity biases are T_eff shifts of -142 to +200 K, log g shifts of -0.070 to +0.35 dex, and [Fe/H] shifts of -0.055 to +0.13 dex. The sample reproduces known trends of increasing binary fraction with higher primary mass and lower metallicity.
AI.conclusion: Unresolved binaries must be accounted for in stellar population modelling and spectroscopic survey interpretation, especially in low-metallicity systems and populations dominated by massive stars.

title: Hidden Disruption in Milky Way-like Satellite Galaxy Populations
comment: 34 pages, 22 figures, submitted to OJA
summary: Determining whether a satellite galaxy is tidally disrupting from photometric observations alone remains a fundamental challenge in near-field cosmology. Cosmological simulations of Milky Way-mass galaxies predict that satellite populations should be highly disrupted, yet the observed Milky Way satellite population appears largely intact. Understanding this tension requires either uncovering disruption that has gone undetected in Milky Way satellites, or identifying limitations in the simulations themselves. We use the Auriga suite of cosmological simulations to evaluate several commonly used indicators of disruption. We find that, in the simulated satellite population, the shape, size, and proper motion alignment of a satellite's bound component are unreliable indicators of its present-day disruption state despite their widespread use in the literature. In contrast, the extended stellar distribution, specifically the ratio of stellar mass between $3r_{1/2}$ and $10r_{1/2}$ to that within $r_{1/2}$, is strongly correlated with disruption. We introduce the extended mass ratio $μ_{\rm EMR}$ as a metric for comparing extended stellar distributions across satellites of varying masses and exploring their connection to disruption in Milky Way observations. Applying this metric to a sample of Milky Way satellites with measured extended stellar distributions, we find that many are consistent with significant ongoing disruption, even among systems traditionally classified as intact. These results suggest that tidal disruption may be substantially more widespread in the observed Milky Way satellite population than currently recognized, and establish extended stellar distributions as a promising new tool for uncovering this hidden disruption.

AI.tldr: Using Auriga cosmological simulations, the authors show that commonly used disruption indicators (bound-component shape, size, proper-motion alignment) are unreliable, whereas the extended stellar distribution—quantified by a new extended mass ratio μ_EMR—correlates strongly with tidal disruption. Applying μ_EMR to Milky Way satellites suggests disruption is more widespread than currently recognized.
AI.motivation: Cosmological simulations of Milky Way-mass galaxies predict heavily disrupted satellite populations, yet observed Milky Way satellites appear largely intact. Resolving this tension requires either detecting previously unrecognized disruption or identifying limitations in the simulations, motivating a systematic test of disruption indicators.
AI.method: The authors use the Auriga suite of cosmological simulations to evaluate several widely used indicators of satellite disruption—bound-component shape, size, and proper-motion alignment—and compare them against actual present-day disruption states. They then define the extended mass ratio μ_EMR, the ratio of stellar mass between 3r_1/2 and 10r_1/2 to that within r_1/2, as a mass-normalized metric of extended stellar distributions, and apply it to Milky Way satellites with measured extended stellar profiles.
AI.result: In the simulated satellite population, shape, size, and proper-motion alignment of the bound component are unreliable indicators of present-day disruption despite their widespread use. In contrast, the extended stellar distribution, specifically μ_EMR, is strongly correlated with disruption. Applying μ_EMR to observed Milky Way satellites reveals that many, including systems traditionally classified as intact, are consistent with significant ongoing disruption.
AI.conclusion: Tidal disruption may be substantially more widespread in the observed Milky Way satellite population than currently recognized. Extended stellar distributions, captured by μ_EMR, offer a promising new tool for uncovering this hidden disruption and for connecting simulations with observations.

title: A Multiwavelength View of SPLUS J102139.31-282247.5: an X-ray Luminous and Eclipsing Dwarf Nova
comment: Accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: We report the independent discovery of the cataclysmic variable (CV) SPLUS J102139.31-282247.5 using Southern Photometric Local Universe Survey 12 band photometry, following its initial identification via ASAS-SN variability. Here, we investigate the system using optical photometry alongside optical and X-ray spectroscopy. High-cadence optical light curves from publicly available TESS data and a dedicated campaign at the Pico dos Dias Observatory in Brazil revealed a highly inclined system exhibiting pronounced eclipses with an orbital period of 1.81 hours. We found no evidence of a WD spin period. Despite seasonal gaps, the long-term ASAS-SN light curve revealed several outbursts (15 with $Δ$mag $\sim$ 1.5 brighter than the mean magnitude) and one superoutburst over the past decade. During Swift X-ray telescope observations, the system exhibited X-ray luminosity of $8.5 \times 10^{31}$ erg s$^{-1}$ in the 0.3-10\,keV band, originating from thermal plasma emission at a temperature consistent with accretion shocks. Optical spectroscopy from the Gemini Multi-Object Spectrographs on the Gemini South telescope confirms the CV nature of the system, showing strong, double-peaked H and HeI emission lines alongside a weak HeII4686 line. Altogether, these features strongly support the classification of SPLUS J102139.31-282247.5 as a quiescent, eclipsing dwarf nova with an unusually high X-ray luminosity.

AI.tldr: Independent discovery and characterization of the cataclysmic variable SPLUS J102139.31-282247.5 as a quiescent eclipsing dwarf nova with an orbital period of 1.81 h and unusually high X-ray luminosity.
AI.motivation: The system was initially flagged via ASAS-SN variability and independently identified in SPLUS 12-band photometry; the authors aim to establish its classification and physical properties through multi-wavelength follow-up.
AI.method: Synthesis of SPLUS 12-band photometry, high-cadence TESS and Pico dos Dias Observatory optical light curves, long-term ASAS-SN photometry, Swift X-ray observations (0.3-10 keV), and Gemini South GMOS optical spectroscopy.
AI.result: A highly inclined system with pronounced eclipses at P=1.81 h and no detected white dwarf spin period; long-term ASAS-SN data show 15 outbursts (Δmag ~1.5) and one superoutburst over a decade; Swift measures L_X = 8.5×10^31 erg/s from thermal plasma at accretion-shock temperatures; GMOS spectra show strong double-peaked H and He I lines with weak He II 4686.
AI.conclusion: The combined photometric, X-ray, and spectroscopic evidence supports classification of SPLUS J102139.31-282247.5 as a quiescent, eclipsing dwarf nova with unusually high X-ray luminosity.

title: The bar-driven central complex of NGC 6946: A panchromatic and spatially resolved view of its star formation history and interstellar medium
comment: Accepted in Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: We present a multi-wavelength analysis of the nearby spiral galaxy NGC 6946, combining optical IFS, infrared, and radio observations. We aim to characterise both the integrated and spatially resolved properties of the stellar populations and ISM, and to interpret them in the context of bar-driven galaxy evolution. We used the SED fitting code SINOPSIS to derive stellar population properties, and different prescriptions to derive ISM properties including atomic and molecular gas masses and the dust mass,temperature, and emissivity index. We find that the central 2.6 kpc hosts $40\%$ of the stellar mass, as well as the bulk of the molecular gas and dust, and has sustained enhanced star formation over cosmic time. A major star formation episode occurred 0.6 Gyr ago. The spatially resolved KS relation shows that molecular gas alone explains only part of the current SFR variance, while alternative prescriptions incorporating stellar mass and dynamical equilibrium pressure yield only modest improvements. We also find radial enhancements in the effective oxygen yield and gas mass fraction relative to surrounding regions, consistent with sustained gas accumulation. Together with the molecular gas streaming motions previously detected kinematic studies, our results are consistent with, and provide independent support for, the inward transport of gas driven by a system of nested bars and with a scenario in which a recent episode of bar-driven gas inflow enhanced the central molecular gas reservoir and sustained elevated star formation. These findings point to efficient HI-to-H$_2$ conversion, likely promoted by the combined effect of the secondary bar and the large dust content, ultimately regulating star formation. We also find indications consistent with a young stellar bar. The current decline in star formation despite large gas reservoirs suggests recent bar-driven quenching.

AI.tldr: A multi-wavelength study of NGC 6946 shows that nested bars have funneled gas into its central 2.6 kpc, fueling an enhanced central starburst ~0.6 Gyr ago via efficient HI-to-H2 conversion, and the galaxy now appears to be entering a bar-driven quenching phase.
AI.motivation: To characterize integrated and spatially resolved stellar population and ISM properties of the nearby spiral NGC 6946 and interpret them within the framework of bar-driven galaxy evolution.
AI.method: Combined optical integral field spectroscopy (IFS), infrared, and radio observations. Stellar population properties were derived with the SED fitting code SINOPSIS; ISM properties (atomic and molecular gas masses, dust mass, temperature, emissivity index) were derived using multiple prescriptions. Star formation was compared to gas via spatially resolved Kennicutt-Schmidt (KS) relations, including prescriptions with stellar mass and dynamical equilibrium pressure.
AI.result: The central 2.6 kpc contains 40% of the stellar mass plus most of the molecular gas and dust, with a major star formation episode at 0.6 Gyr ago. The resolved KS relation shows molecular gas explains only part of the SFR variance, with stellar mass/dynamical pressure prescriptions giving modest improvements. Radial enhancements in effective oxygen yield and gas mass fraction indicate sustained gas accumulation; together with previously detected molecular gas streaming motions, this independently supports inward transport driven by nested bars. Findings suggest efficient HI-to-H2 conversion (promoted by the secondary bar and large dust content) regulating star formation, indications of a young stellar bar, and recent bar-driven quenching.
AI.conclusion: Nested bars have efficiently transported gas inward, building the central molecular reservoir and sustaining elevated star formation, with the current SFR decline despite large gas reservoirs pointing to bar-driven quenching, offering independent support for bar-driven evolutionary scenarios.

title: Gaia in Technicolor. I. A Simple Variability-Encoded Color-Magnitude Diagram
comment: 19 pages, 13 figures. Submitted to Publications of the Astronomical Society of the Pacific
summary: The Hertzsprung-Russell diagram is one of the most important tools in stellar astrophysics. In its modern, empirical form as the Gaia color-magnitude diagram (CMD), each star is represented with a point determined from its time-averaged brightness and color. However, many stars are intrinsically variable, and the fixed-point representation ignores the variety of ways in which a star can vary. As a system pulsates, eclipses, is irradiated, erupts, or otherwise varies, it moves through the CMD along a trajectory whose size, slope, and shape are determined by the physics driving the brightness and color variability. Here we exploit the near-simultaneous, three-band, multi-epoch photometry (MEP) released for ~11.7 million sources in Gaia DR3 to construct a variability-encoded CMD (VECMD). In this updated take on the traditional CMD, each star is represented not by a point but by a linear segment approximating the path it traces in absolute magnitude and color as it varies. Because these trajectories are built from the raw epoch data, they are agnostic to period and do not require phase-folding. We show that radial-mode pulsators trace looped, Lissajous-like trajectories that can encode the phase lag between radius and temperature. The Hertzsprung bump is even visible in the CMD loops of some Cepheids. Variable binary systems can trace tight color-correlated lines and/or hooked paths. Accreting and dust-obscured systems trace long, high-amplitude tracks aligned with the outburst or reddening vector. Distinct regions of the VECMD are dominated by distinct trajectory morphologies. We argue that these trajectories are period-independent fingerprints well suited to machine learning classification, which we will pursue on the much larger epoch-photometry sample expected in Gaia DR4. Finally, we present a free app called IVECMD for finding, classifying, and analyzing variable stars in the VECMD.

AI.tldr: The authors build a variability-encoded color-magnitude diagram (VECMD) from Gaia DR3 multi-epoch photometry, replacing each star's fixed point with a linear segment tracing its trajectory in absolute magnitude and color, and show that trajectory morphology is a period-independent fingerprint for classification.
AI.motivation: The traditional Gaia color-magnitude diagram represents each star as a single point from time-averaged brightness and color, which discards the intrinsic variability of many stars and the physical information encoded in how they move through the diagram.
AI.method: Uses near-simultaneous three-band multi-epoch photometry (MEP) for ~11.7 million sources in Gaia DR3 to construct a VECMD, in which each star is represented by a linear segment approximating its path in absolute magnitude and color. Trajectories are built directly from raw epoch data, so they are agnostic to period and avoid phase-folding.
AI.result: Radial-mode pulsators trace looped, Lissajous-like trajectories encoding the phase lag between radius and temperature, with the Hertzsprung bump visible in CMD loops of some Cepheids. Variable binaries show tight color-correlated lines and hooked paths; accreting and dust-obscured systems trace long, high-amplitude tracks aligned with outburst or reddening vectors. Distinct VECMD regions are dominated by distinct trajectory morphologies.
AI.conclusion: Trajectory shapes are period-independent fingerprints well suited to machine-learning classification, to be pursued on the larger epoch-photometry sample expected in Gaia DR4. A free app, IVECMD, is presented for finding, classifying, and analyzing variable stars in the VECMD.

title: Contrasting geometries of kiloparsec-scale stellar flows associated with giant Galactic cavities
comment: 40 pages, 4 main figures and 5 Extended Data figures; Supplementary Information included
summary: Giant bubbles and cavities are widespread in star-forming galactic discs, yet the stellar dynamics associated with such structures remain poorly constrained. Here we combine Gaia Data Release 3 with three-dimensional extinction information to identify 3,502 massive-star candidates corresponding to initial masses $M_{\rm ini}\gtrsim8\,M_{\odot}$ within 5 kpc of the Sun. A search of the stellar-density field alone, independent of interstellar-medium morphology and stellar kinematics, reveals two prominent overdensities, R1 and R2, with characteristic scales of approximately 1.3 kpc. Both are subsequently found to be associated with previously identified giant interstellar cavities in projected position and line-of-sight location. After subtracting locally fitted background velocity fields, stars with full three-dimensional velocities reveal coherent divergent in-plane motions across both structures. R1 extends well beyond a known massive-star association and exhibits strongly anisotropic expansion, with one principal strain rate robustly positive and the other consistent with zero. R2 instead exhibits positive strain rates along both principal directions, indicating broadly two-dimensional internal expansion. These results show that density-selected, cavity-associated stellar structures of comparable scale can host coherent kiloparsec-scale flows with contrasting internal flow geometries and need not share a common stellar kinematic organisation.

AI.tldr: Using Gaia DR3 plus 3D extinction data, the authors identify two ~1.3 kpc massive-star overdensities (R1, R2) in the solar neighbourhood that coincide with known giant interstellar cavities. Both show coherent divergent in-plane motions, but with contrasting anisotropy: R1 expands strongly along one principal axis only, while R2 expands along both.
AI.motivation: Giant bubbles and cavities are ubiquitous in star-forming galactic discs, but the stellar kinematics associated with these structures are poorly constrained. The paper aims to link density-selected massive-star structures to known interstellar cavities and characterise their large-scale stellar flows.
AI.method: Combines Gaia DR3 astrometry with three-dimensional extinction information to select 3,502 massive-star candidates (initial mass ≳8 M_sun) within 5 kpc. Performs a purely density-field search (independent of ISM morphology and kinematics) to detect overdensities, cross-matches them in projected position and line of sight with known giant cavities, then subtracts locally fitted background velocity fields to extract coherent 3D stellar motions and principal strain rates.
AI.result: Two overdensities, R1 and R2, both ~1.3 kpc in scale, are found and associated with previously identified giant interstellar cavities. After background subtraction, both show coherent divergent in-plane motions. R1 extends beyond a known massive-star association and shows strongly anisotropic expansion (one principal strain rate robustly positive, the other consistent with zero); R2 shows positive strain rates along both principal directions, indicating broadly 2D internal expansion.
AI.conclusion: Density-selected, cavity-associated stellar structures of comparable scale can host coherent kiloparsec-scale flows with contrasting internal flow geometries, and need not share a common stellar kinematic organisation.

title: Extended J-band spectroscopy of red supergiants: parameter identifiability and metallicity robustness
comment: Comments: 20 pages, 6 figures, accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: Red supergiants (RSGs) provide a near-infrared metallicity diagnostic complementary to optical hot-supergiant spectroscopy, but their low-resolution extragalactic use requires tests of parameter identifiability and modelling robustness. We quantify the information content of extended J-band RSG spectra at R=2000 over 1.155-1.340 um and assess recovery of effective temperature, surface gravity, microturbulence, and metallicity. Using MARCS/TURBOSPECTRUM spectra and an emulator, we perform a six-node Fisher analysis and controlled mock experiments, and analyse 21 SpeX spectra of 20 RSG candidates towards Per OB1. All four parameters produce measurable responses, but only 8-10% of the raw metallicity information and 4-7% of the gravity information are independent of the other parameter directions. Extending beyond 1.22 um provides median fractions of 60% of the raw and 66% of the nuisance-orthogonal metallicity information. Gravity dominates the weakest Fisher mode, while its prior choice shifts association means by at most 0.03 dex. Matched mocks recover metallicity with an rms error of 0.04 dex. Standard continuum treatment biases solar-metallicity mocks by about -0.23 dex, reduced to about -0.01 dex by our adopted treatment. Plausible CNO mismatch adds a zero-point sensitivity of 0.04-0.05 dex, and regularised covariance changes association means by at most 0.03 dex. The preferred analysis gives a mean [Z] = -0.10 dex with a star-to-star dispersion of 0.09 dex. Extended low-resolution J-band spectra therefore yield recoverable metallicity and temperature constraints once continuum placement and weak parameter directions are controlled, although the absolute scale remains conditional on the adopted atmosphere and line-formation framework.

AI.tldr: Extended low-resolution J-band RSG spectra at R=2000 can recover metallicity and temperature once continuum placement and weak parameter directions are controlled, but the absolute scale remains model-dependent.
AI.motivation: Red supergiants offer a near-infrared metallicity diagnostic complementary to optical hot-supergiant spectroscopy, yet extragalactic low-resolution use requires validation of parameter identifiability and modelling robustness.
AI.method: Uses MARCS/TURBOSPECTRUM spectra with an emulator, a six-node Fisher analysis, controlled mock experiments, and analysis of 21 SpeX spectra of 20 RSG candidates toward Per OB1 to quantify information content of J-band spectra (1.155-1.340 um, R=2000) for Teff, log g, microturbulence, and metallicity.
AI.result: All four parameters show measurable responses, but only 8-10% of raw metallicity information and 4-7% of gravity information are independent of other directions; beyond 1.22 um yields 60% raw and 66% nuisance-orthogonal metallicity information. Gravity dominates the weakest Fisher mode (prior shifts <=0.03 dex), matched mocks recover metallicity to 0.04 dex rms, standard continuum treatment biases solar mocks by -0.23 dex (reduced to -0.01 dex with adopted treatment), CNO mismatch adds 0.04-0.05 dex zero-point sensitivity, and regularised covariance shifts means <=0.03 dex. Preferred analysis gives mean [Z] = -0.10 dex with 0.09 dex dispersion.
AI.conclusion: Extended low-resolution J-band RSG spectra yield recoverable metallicity and temperature constraints when continuum placement and weak parameter directions are controlled, though the absolute scale remains conditional on the adopted atmosphere and line-formation framework.

title: The Magnetized Universe: From planet-forming disks to the high-redshift universe
comment: Part of the ALMA2040 White Paper Series. 8 pages, 2 figures
summary: The interstellar medium (ISM) is magnetized at all scales and phases in our Galaxy and other galaxies across the Universe. Spectro-polarimetric millimetre observations are essential to probe the role of the interstellar magnetic fields in the dynamics of the cold universe, and how this affects the star formation process, and planet formation in nearby star forming regions. Such observations are also essential for understanding magnetic fields in active stars and the shaping and evolution of the circumstellar environments of evolved stars. While ALMA has been revolutionary in advancing our knowledge about magnetic fields in the ISM, the limitations in calibration, especially for circular polarization, and sensitivity for large samples, have hindered robust measurements of field strengths, which are essential for fully assessing their role in ISM dynamics. An ALMA2040 that broadens spectro-polarimetric capabilities to include robust circular calibration and increases sensitivity with more collecting area will enable crucial observations of magnetic fields across the Universe and over a wide range of spatial scales to fully ascertain the influences of magnetic fields from galaxy assembly to forming planets.

AI.tldr: This white paper argues that broadening ALMA's spectro-polarimetric capabilities—robust circular polarization calibration and greater collecting area (sensitivity)—is essential to measure magnetic field strengths across the ISM and thereby assess the role of magnetic fields from galaxy assembly to planet formation.
AI.motivation: The ISM is magnetized at all scales and phases, and magnetic fields likely influence cold-universe dynamics, star formation, planet formation in nearby regions, active stars, and evolved-star circumstellar environments. Field strength measurements are needed to assess these roles, but current ALMA limitations in calibration (especially circular polarization) and sensitivity for large samples hinder robust measurements.
AI.method: A community white paper (ALMA2040 vision) making the science case for expanded spectro-polarimetric millimetre observations: advocating robust circular polarization calibration and increased sensitivity via more collecting area.
AI.result: No new observational results are reported; the paper synthesizes the current state—ALMA has been revolutionary for ISM magnetic field studies, yet calibration and sensitivity constraints currently prevent robust field-strength measurements over large samples.
AI.conclusion: An ALMA2040 with robust circular calibration and greater collecting area would enable crucial magnetic field observations across the Universe and over a wide range of spatial scales, fully ascertaining magnetic field influences from galaxy assembly to forming planets.

title: The GAGE survey. I. Deep multi-band stellar variability characterization and automated classification toward Baade's window
summary: Context. Long-term photometric surveys of the Galactic bulge are vital for characterizing its stellar populations and structure, providing a foundation for next-generation facilities. Aims. We present initial results of the GalActic bulGe with plEiadi (GAGE) project, focusing on variable star discovery in Baade's Window. Methods. Using archival DECam (ugriz) data on the Blanco 4-m Telescope spanning six years, we applied high-precision PSF photometry. We developed a pipeline combining Generalized Lomb-Scargle analysis and polynomial light-curve modelling to derive mean multi-band magnitudes and amplitudes. Results. Quality cuts yield 6,304 high-confidence variable sources. We expand multi-band coverage for 4,568 sources in common with OGLE IV and uncover 1,736 (~28%) new candidates absent from OGLE IV. Using a Random Forest classifier, we categorize these sources, finding that 1,391 were also missing from both Gaia DR3 and VVV. This population is concentrated at the fainter end (i >= 17.5 mag), enabled by our deeper detection limits. Conclusions. Our pipeline effectively probes deep, highly crowded fields, expanding the variable star inventory of the inner Galaxy as a benchmark for Rubin-LSST.

AI.tldr: The GAGE project reports a DECam-based variable star census in Baade's Window, yielding 6,304 high-confidence variables, including 1,736 new candidates absent from OGLE IV and 1,391 undetected in both Gaia DR3 and VVV.
AI.motivation: Long-term photometric surveys of the Galactic bulge are essential for characterizing its stellar populations and structure and for laying groundwork for next-generation facilities; deep, crowded-field variable discovery in Baade's Window remains incomplete at faint magnitudes.
AI.method: Archival six-year DECam ugriz data from the Blanco 4-m Telescope were processed with high-precision PSF photometry; a pipeline combining Generalized Lomb-Scargle period analysis with polynomial light-curve modelling derived mean multi-band magnitudes and amplitudes, and a Random Forest classifier categorized the sources.
AI.result: Quality cuts yield 6,304 high-confidence variables. Multi-band coverage is extended for 4,568 sources in common with OGLE IV, and 1,736 (~28%) new candidates absent from OGLE IV are found; 1,391 of these are also missing from Gaia DR3 and VVV, concentrated at the faint end (i >= 17.5 mag) owing to deeper detection limits.
AI.conclusion: The pipeline effectively probes deep, highly crowded fields, expanding the inner-Galaxy variable star inventory and providing a benchmark dataset for Rubin-LSST.

title: Dust in Galaxies at $z=10-15$: Attenuation and Re-emission Predictions from the FirstLight Simulations
comment: 30 pages, submitted to ApJ on October 15, 2026. The main results are presented in Figures 9, 11, and 16. Comments are welcome
summary: Dust masses and grain properties in $z>10$ galaxies remain poorly constrained, as JWST UV attenuation and ALMA dust re-emission are rarely modelled consistently. We perform post-processed 3D dust radiative transfer on 208 snapshots of 99 galaxies at $z=10$-15 from the FirstLight simulations ($M_*=10^{6.5}$-$10^{9.5}\,M_\odot$), applying twelve dust models per snapshot (2496 runs): four dust-to-metal (DTM) prescriptions and three grain size distributions. Metallicity-dependent DTM models reproduce ALMA dust-mass upper limits at $z\gtrsim10$ and detections at $z\sim7$, as dust-to-stellar mass ratios rise sharply near $Z\sim0.2\,Z_\odot$, typically at $M_*\gtrsim10^{8.5}\,M_\odot$, where grain growth by metal accretion becomes dominant. A constant DTM of 0.4 instead violates more than half of the upper limits. For dust attenuation, SMC-like dust is favored by the observed $M_{\rm UV}$-$β_{\rm UV}$ relation. The observed UV slopes ($β_{\rm UV}\simeq-2.3$) favor small grains ($a\lesssimλ_{\rm UV}/2π\simeq0.025\,μ{\rm m}$) producing steep UV extinction, together with a low abundance of carbonaceous grains or PAHs responsible for the 2175 $\mathrm{\mathring{A}}$ bump, consistent with silicate-rich dust. Large-grain stellar dust ($a_0=0.1\,μ{\rm m}$) instead yields nearly grey extinction and UV slopes close to the intrinsic value ($β_{\rm UV,0}\simeq-2.6$). SMC and MW attenuation curves flatten at $A_{\rm V}\gtrsim0.3$, showing that relatively flat attenuation does not necessarily imply large grains. For dust re-emission, dust peak temperatures reach 60-80 K, exceeding the 40-50 K commonly assumed in ALMA dust-mass estimates. Predicted IR continuum flux increases with UV luminosity; at current ALMA sensitivities (10-20 $μ$Jy), detections generally require $M_{\rm UV}\lesssim-21.5$. Roman wide-field surveys may identify such rare UV-bright galaxies.

AI.tldr: Post-processed 3D dust radiative transfer on 2496 model runs (99 FirstLight galaxies at z=10-15, 12 dust models each) shows that metallicity-dependent dust-to-metal ratios reproduce ALMA dust-mass limits, SMC-like small silicate grains match observed UV slopes, and dust temperatures reach 60-80 K, higher than typical ALMA assumptions.
AI.motivation: Dust masses and grain properties in z>10 galaxies are poorly constrained because JWST UV attenuation and ALMA dust re-emission are rarely modeled consistently within a single framework.
AI.method: The authors perform post-processed 3D dust radiative transfer on 208 snapshots of 99 galaxies at z=10-15 from the FirstLight simulations (M*=10^6.5-10^9.5 Msun), applying twelve dust models per snapshot (2496 runs total): four dust-to-metal (DTM) prescriptions and three grain size distributions, and compare predictions to observed M_UV-beta_UV relations and ALMA dust-mass constraints.
AI.result: Metallicity-dependent DTM models reproduce ALMA dust-mass upper limits at z>~10 and detections at z~7, with dust-to-stellar mass ratios rising sharply near Z~0.2 Zsun (typically M*>~10^8.5 Msun) where metal-accretion grain growth dominates; a constant DTM of 0.4 violates over half the upper limits. SMC-like dust is favored by the M_UV-beta_UV relation; observed beta_UV~-2.3 favors small grains (a<~0.025 um) with steep UV extinction and low carbonaceous/PAH abundance (silicate-rich dust), whereas large grains (a0=0.1 um) give grey extinction and beta_UV~-2.6. SMC/MW curves flatten at A_V>~0.3. Dust peak temperatures reach 60-80 K, exceeding the 40-50 K commonly assumed.
AI.conclusion: Consistent UV-attenuation and IR re-emission modeling favors metallicity-dependent DTM, SMC-like small silicate-rich grains, and warmer dust than typically assumed; at current ALMA sensitivities (10-20 uJy) detections require M_UV<~-21.5, and Roman wide-field surveys may find such rare UV-bright galaxies.

title: A Neural Network - Based Tool for Rapid Orbital Solution of Contact Binary Systems
comment: 13 pages, 8 figures, 3 tables, accepted by ApJ
summary: With the rapid growth of large-scale time-domain surveys, vast amounts of photometric and spectroscopic data are continuously being released. A substantial number of contact binaries have been identified, accompanied by both light curves and radial velocity observations. Traditional modeling of these datasets relies on computationally intensive physical models, which limits their applicability to large-scale analyses. To this end, this paper proposes the use of a fully connected neural network and a SIREN (Sitzmann et al. 2020) model to rapidly generate radial velocity curves. After training, the models can rapidly generate radial velocity curves with high accuracy, significantly reducing computational costs and enabling efficient large-scale studies. This method was further integrated with the light curve computation framework developed by Li et al. (2025), allowing simultaneous fitting of radial velocities and light curves. To assess the reliability of the proposed model, synthetic observational datasets were constructed and used for parameter estimation. The deviations between the derived parameters and the ground-truth values were analyzed quantitatively, enabling a comprehensive evaluation of the model's accuracy.

AI.tldr: A fully connected neural network and a SIREN model are trained to rapidly emulate radial velocity curves of contact binaries, replacing expensive physical modeling, and are integrated with a light-curve framework for joint RV + light-curve fitting validated on synthetic data.
AI.motivation: Large time-domain surveys release vast photometric and spectroscopic data, including many contact binaries with both light curves and radial velocity observations. Traditional physical modeling is computationally intensive, limiting large-scale analysis.
AI.method: Train a fully connected neural network and a SIREN-based model to generate radial velocity curves from parameters, then integrate the emulator with Li et al. (2025)'s light curve computation framework to enable simultaneous fitting of radial velocities and light curves. Reliability is assessed via synthetic observational datasets and quantitative comparison of estimated parameters against ground truth.
AI.result: After training, the models rapidly produce radial velocity curves with high accuracy, substantially reducing computational cost. Parameter estimation on synthetic datasets shows quantifiable small deviations from ground-truth values, supporting the emulator's accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Neural-network surrogates (FCNN and SIREN) enable fast, accurate radial velocity curve generation and can be combined with light-curve modeling for efficient joint fitting, making large-scale contact binary analyses feasible.

title: $\texttt{GASTRO-BH}$: Effects of a Central Black Hole in GSE-like Dwarf-galaxy Mergers Around Milky Way-like Hosts
comment: 23 pages, 11 figures. Comments are welcome! Submitted to ApJ
summary: Recent evidence points to an intermediate-mass black hole (IMBH) in the most massive globular cluster of the Milky Way, $ω$ Centauri. This globular cluster is commonly associated with the Gaia-Sausage/Enceladus (GSE) dwarf galaxy, the last major merger event of our Galaxy, as its nuclear star cluster remnant. Motivated by this, we investigate whether the interaction between a bright GSE-like dwarf galaxy with stellar mass in the range $10^{8.5}$--$10^{9.7}$ solar masses and a Milky Way-like host can either suppress or enhance the growth of a central black hole (BH) during the merger process. To this end, we perform high-resolution $N$-body and smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) simulations with the ChaNGa framework and a modified, angular-momentum-aware Bondi-Hoyle accretion prescription, considering both isolated dwarf galaxies and merger simulations with different stellar feedback efficiencies. The merger simulations show that the interaction does not halt BH accretion; instead, tidal interactions and gas inflows during pericentric passages strongly enhance accretion, leading to BH mass growth by more than two orders of magnitude in both low- and high-feedback models. The enhanced accretion is accompanied by suppressed star formation in the dwarf galaxy. Our results suggest that mergers similar to the GSE event can efficiently fuel IMBH growth in satellite galaxies rather than suppress it. This may be in tension with the estimated low mass of the proposed IMBH in $ω$ Centauri, but it could provide a mechanism for triggering active galactic nucleus activity in dwarf galaxies.

AI.tldr: Merger with a Milky Way-like host enhances, rather than suppresses, central black hole growth in a GSE-like dwarf galaxy by over two orders of magnitude, potentially in tension with the low mass of the proposed IMBH in ω Centauri.
AI.motivation: Evidence for an intermediate-mass black hole (IMBH) in ω Centauri, which is associated with the Gaia-Sausage/Enceladus (GSE) dwarf galaxy, motivates testing whether a GSE-like dwarf-host merger suppresses or enhances central black hole growth.
AI.method: High-resolution N-body and smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) simulations using the ChaNGa framework with a modified, angular-momentum-aware Bondi-Hoyle accretion prescription, covering isolated dwarf galaxies and merger simulations with varying stellar feedback efficiencies, for dwarf stellar masses of 10^8.5–10^9.7 solar masses.
AI.result: Mergers do not halt BH accretion; tidal interactions and gas inflows during pericentric passages strongly enhance accretion, growing the BH mass by more than two orders of magnitude in both low- and high-feedback models, accompanied by suppressed star formation in the dwarf.
AI.conclusion: Mergers like the GSE event can efficiently fuel IMBH growth in satellite galaxies rather than suppress it, potentially in tension with the estimated low mass of the proposed IMBH in ω Centauri, but offering a mechanism for triggering AGN activity in dwarf galaxies.

title: A Hectospec Spectroscopic Census of Kinematic Members in the Orion Nebula Cluster
comment: 23 pages, 15 figures and 10 tables (including tables in apenddices)
summary: We present a comprehensive spectroscopic census of the Orion Nebula Cluster (ONC), based primarily on low-resolution optical spectroscopy obtained with MMT/Hectospec. We derive spectral types, youth indicators, and accretion diagnostics for 1513 stars located in the ONC region, enabling the identification and characterization of pre-main-sequence stars. We combine these measurements with a kinematic membership analysis based on Gaia Data Release 3 astrometry to identify and confirm cluster members. Using these combined diagnostics, we identify and characterize 780 bona fide T Tauri stars associated with the ONC. In addition, we construct a census of protoplanetary discs using infrared photometry obtained with the IRAC and MIPS instruments aboard the Spitzer Space Telescope. We further derive stellar masses, ages, and extinctions using the MassAge code, which combines photometric and spectroscopic inputs with stellar evolutionary models, and employs a Monte Carlo approach for uncertainty propagation. The resulting homogeneous catalogue of ONC members provides spectroscopic characterizations, kinematic membership constraints, disc diagnostics, and self-consistent estimates of stellar physical parameters. This dataset offers a refined view of the stellar population of the ONC and provides a robust foundation for investigating its kinematic structure, age distribution, and protoplanetary disc population.

AI.tldr: A large homogeneous spectroscopic catalogue of 1513 stars in the Orion Nebula Cluster yields 780 confirmed T Tauri members, with spectral types, youth/accretion diagnostics, kinematic membership from Gaia DR3, disc census from Spitzer IRAC/MIPS, and stellar masses, ages and extinctions from the MassAge Monte Carlo tool.
AI.motivation: The Orion Nebula Cluster is a key laboratory for pre-main-sequence stellar populations and disc evolution, but needs a homogeneous, membership-controlled census that combines spectroscopy, kinematics and multi-wavelength photometry to reliably identify cluster members and characterize their youth, accretion, discs and physical parameters.
AI.method: Low-resolution optical spectroscopy with MMT/Hectospec for 1513 ONC-region stars to derive spectral types, youth indicators and accretion diagnostics; Gaia DR3 astrometry for kinematic membership analysis; Spitzer IRAC and MIPS infrared photometry to build a protoplanetary-disc census; MassAge code combining photometric and spectroscopic inputs with stellar evolutionary models and Monte Carlo uncertainty propagation to derive masses, ages and extinctions.
AI.result: Spectral and membership diagnostics identify and characterize 780 bona fide T Tauri stars associated with the ONC, plus a disc census and self-consistent mass, age and extinction estimates for the sample.
AI.conclusion: The study delivers a homogeneous catalogue of ONC members with spectroscopic characterization, kinematic membership constraints, disc diagnostics and consistent stellar parameters, offering a refined view of the ONC stellar population and a robust foundation for studying its kinematic structure, age distribution and protoplanetary disc population.

title: $N$-body simulations of the open cluster M67 -- I: global cluster properties
comment: 14 pages, 11 figures. Submitted to MNRAS
summary: The most recent Gaia data releases have seen the construction of many open cluster catalogues containing thousands of open clusters. Simulations of these clusters are needed in order to interpret observations, both existing and upcoming. M67 is an ideal open cluster to calibrate these simulations due to its advanced age and large, diverse binary populations. Moreover it is one of the most extensively observed open clusters with observations in several wavelengths. We aim to reproduce the global cluster properties of M67 with modern $N$-body simulations, as well as comparing its observed properties in the largest homogeneous open cluster catalogue with other available observations. We carry out several NBODY6++GPU simulations with varying initial conditions, including metallicity, half-mass radius, and the distribution of orbital binary parameters. Our models broadly reproduce the observed global properties of M67, and we are able to recreate the cluster's surface brightness profile, radial mass profile, and colour-magnitude diagram. Our favoured model indicates an initial half-mass radius of around 1.6 pc, although its total observable cluster mass may be too high. Further simulations are planned for a subsequent study, with a focus on recreating the present-day binary populations of M67.

AI.tldr: Direct N-body (NBODY6++GPU) simulations of M67 with varied metallicity, half-mass radius, and binary orbital parameters broadly reproduce the cluster's observed global properties, favouring an initial half-mass radius of ~1.6 pc.
AI.motivation: Recent Gaia releases yield large open-cluster catalogues of thousands of clusters, and interpreting these (existing and upcoming) observations requires calibrated simulations. M67, with its advanced age, large and diverse binary populations, and extensive multi-wavelength observations, is an ideal calibrator.
AI.method: The authors run several NBODY6++GPU N-body simulations varying initial conditions: metallicity, half-mass radius, and the distribution of orbital binary parameters. They then compare outputs against the largest homogeneous open-cluster catalogue and other available observations of M67.
AI.result: Models broadly reproduce M67's observed global properties, including the surface brightness profile, radial mass profile, and colour-magnitude diagram. The favoured model implies an initial half-mass radius of ~1.6 pc, though its total observable cluster mass may be too high.
AI.conclusion: N-body simulations can reproduce M67's global observable properties, supporting its use as a calibration benchmark; the preferred model has an initial half-mass radius of ~1.6 pc but possibly overestimates total observable mass. A follow-up study will focus on reproducing the present-day binary populations.

title: Survey of Orion Disks with ALMA (SODA) IV: Millimeter variability of protoplanetary disks
comment: Accepted by A&A on 12/10/2026
summary: Context. Short-term millimeter-wavelength variability in Class II young stellar objects (YSOs) has been considered minimal, often dismissed as very rare in ALMA-based studies on short timescales. However, recent findings suggest that variability on sub-day timescales is significant. Aims. This study aims to quantify short timescale (~1 hour to ~3 days) millimeter flux variability in unresolved Class II YSO disks observed as part of the SODA survey, leveraging its large dataset to assess the statistical significance of such variability across the LDN 1641 and LDN 1647 regions in Orion. Methods. We analyze ALMA Band 6 observations of 873 YSOs obtained over multiple epochs using a custom flux extraction pipeline to separate individual execution blocks. By computing variability factors and statistical deviations from the mean flux, we identify sources exhibiting significant variability, accounting for noise and calibrator stability. Results. Even with conservative selection criteria, we identify 20 variable sources within the sample (~5.3% of all detections). The maximum of the measured variability factor is >=7 over about one hour. More liberal selection criteria yield up to 60 sources that could be called potentially variable (~15.9%). Conclusions. The number of variable sources detected in our sample indicates physical processes operating on time scales of hours, likely associated with magnetic reconnection and/or synchrotron radiation or strong cases of magnetic accretion changes. These detections show the need to reconsider typical stability assumptions in single-epoch observations and calls for follow-up studies in star-forming regions with ALMA. Masses derived from unresolved measurements could potentially be biased by this sort of variability.

AI.tldr: ALMA Band 6 multi-epoch observations of 873 Class II YSOs in Orion reveal that short-timescale (hour-to-day) millimeter flux variability is more common than previously assumed, with ~5.3% (conservatively) up to ~15.9% of sources variable.
AI.motivation: Short-term millimeter variability in Class II YSOs has traditionally been deemed minimal or very rare in ALMA studies, but recent evidence suggests significant sub-day variability. The authors exploit the large SODA survey dataset to test this assumption statistically and to determine whether such variability is a genuine, widespread phenomenon rather than an isolated curiosity.
AI.method: Analysis of ALMA Band 6 observations of 873 unresolved Class II YSOs in LDN 1641 and LDN 1647 (Orion), spanning multiple epochs. A custom flux-extraction pipeline separates individual execution blocks to enable per-epoch photometry over ~1 hour to ~3 days. Variability factors and statistical deviations from the mean flux are computed, with noise and calibrator stability accounted for; conservative and liberal selection criteria are applied to classify variable and potentially variable sources.
AI.result: Under conservative criteria, 20 variable sources are identified (~5.3% of all detections), with a maximum variability factor of >=7 over ~1 hour. More liberal criteria yield up to 60 potentially variable sources (~15.9%).
AI.conclusion: Hour-scale millimeter variability is present at a statistically meaningful level, implying physical processes operating on hours—plausibly magnetic reconnection, synchrotron radiation, or strong magnetic accretion changes. The results challenge the standard stability assumptions underlying single-epoch observations, motivate ALMA follow-up monitoring in star-forming regions, and warn that masses derived from unresolved measurements may be biased by such variability.

title: How bright can a galaxy be? Extreme value predictions for high-redshift survey observables
comment: 15 pages, 10 figures. Submitted to MNRAS. Comments welcome!
summary: Assessing the significance of extreme galaxy candidates has typically relied on redshifts and stellar / halo masses inferred through inverse modelling, which carries substantial systematic uncertainty. We combine the halo mass function with a conditional model for galaxy emission and apply the Extreme Value Statistics (EVS) formalism to predict the distribution of the observed flux of the brightest galaxy expected in a given survey area, redshift interval and photometric band. We find the choice of parametric star formation history (SFH) dominates the modelling uncertainty, introducing a spread approaching $\sim 1 \, \mathrm{dex}$ by $z \sim 18$, whilst the stellar population synthesis model, initial mass function and metallicity each contribute $\lesssim 0.3 \, \mathrm{dex}$. The luminous $z \gtrsim 9$ candidates in COSMOS-Web cluster about the median prediction for the area they were drawn from, and lie at least an order of magnitude below the $3σ$ limit, a margin comparable to the SFH systematic. Of the observational samples reaching beyond $z \sim 13$, the two spectroscopically confirmed galaxies at $z \simeq 14$ lie close to the median prediction for their area, whereas photometric candidates at $z \gtrsim 16$ reach $+4σ$ (a probability to exceed of $\sim 10^{-5}$), the brightest lying at the limit obtained by converting all halo baryons into stars. Since the prediction bounds the flux far more tightly than the photometry bounds the redshift, such offsets are most naturally resolved by errors in the inferred redshifts. This approach allows extreme candidates to be assessed directly in the observational plane, making explicit the modelling assumptions common to forward and inverse approaches.

AI.tldr: The authors combine the halo mass function with a conditional galaxy-emission model and Extreme Value Statistics to predict the brightest-galaxy flux distribution directly in the observational plane, finding that SFH choice dominates modelling uncertainty (~1 dex by z~18) and that an absolute-magnitude/flux-space assessment is a sharper diagnostic of extreme candidates than redshift inference.
AI.motivation: Assessments of extreme high-redshift galaxy candidates typically rest on redshifts and stellar/halo masses obtained by inverse modelling, which carries large systematic uncertainties. The authors seek a forward, observational-plane framework that makes modelling assumptions explicit and separates them from photometric inference errors.
AI.method: Couple the halo mass function with a conditional model for galaxy emission, then apply Extreme Value Statistics (EVS) to predict the distribution of observed flux of the brightest galaxy expected for a given survey area, redshift interval and photometric band. They quantify systematic budget across parametric star formation history (SFH), stellar population synthesis model, IMF and metallicity, and compare predictions with observed samples (COSMOS-Web z≳9, spectroscopically confirmed z≈14 objects, photometric candidates at z≳16).
AI.result: The choice of parametric SFH dominates the modelling uncertainty, producing a spread approaching ~1 dex by z~18, while SPS model, IMF and metallicity each contribute ≲0.3 dex. Luminous z≳9 COSMOS-Web candidates cluster around the median prediction for their survey area and lie at least an order of magnitude below the 3σ limit, a margin comparable to the SFH systematic. Of samples beyond z~13, the two spectroscopically confirmed z≈14 galaxies sit near the median prediction, whereas photometric candidates at z≳16 reach +4σ (probability to exceed ~10^-5), the brightest approaching the limit obtained by converting all halo baryons into stars.
AI.conclusion: Because the EVS prediction constrains flux far more tightly than photometry constrains redshift, apparent offsets for the most extreme candidates are most naturally attributed to errors in the inferred redshifts. The forward EVS approach enables extreme candidates to be assessed directly in the observational plane while making explicit the modelling assumptions shared with inverse approaches.

title: Characterizing the Martin Luther King Event: Sun to Earth Evolution of the January 19, 2026 Geomagnetic Storm
summary: We present a comprehensive Sun-to-Earth analysis of the extreme space weather event of 18 -19 January 2026, hereafter the Martin Luther King (MLK) storm, which produced a severe (G4) geomagnetic storm and one of the most intense solar radiation storms of Solar Cycle 25. The geomagnetic disturbance was driven by a fast Earth-directed coronal mass ejection (CME) associated with an X1.9-class flare from NOAA Active Region 14341. We combine multi-viewpoint remote-sensing observations, in situ measurements from Solar Orbiter and Wind, and physics-based magnetohydrodynamic simulations using the CORHEL-CME framework to reconstruct the eruption from the low corona to 1 au and identify the mechanisms governing its geoeffectiveness. Observations and simulations indicate that the eruption originated from a right-handed magnetic flux rope embedded in a complex magnetic environment dominated by a neighboring positive-polarity coronal hole. The simulations reproduce the observed CME morphology, asymmetric expansion, magnetic fields measured at both spacecraft, and Dst index evolution. The main discrepancy is attributed to filament material not included in the model. Favorable magnetic polarity alignment between the CME and coronal-hole field minimized magnetic erosion through interchange reconnection, enabling rapid escape and preservation of the strong southward magnetic field that drove the geomagnetic storm. The prolonged recovery phase resulted from interaction between the trailing CME and a following high-speed stream from the same coronal hole. These results demonstrate that storm intensity was primarily established by the coronal magnetic configuration, whereas storm duration was controlled by the ambient solar wind.

AI.tldr: A Sun-to-Earth study of the 18–19 January 2026 "MLK" G4 storm shows that favorable polarity alignment between the CME's right-handed flux rope and a neighboring positive-polarity coronal hole limited magnetic erosion, preserving the southward field that drove the intense geomagnetic storm.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to identify the mechanisms governing the geoeffectiveness of the 18–19 January 2026 MLK event, a severe G4 geomagnetic storm and one of the strongest solar radiation storms of Solar Cycle 25, driven by a fast Earth-directed CME from an X1.9 flare in NOAA AR 14341.
AI.method: The authors combine multi-viewpoint remote-sensing observations, in situ measurements from Solar Orbiter and Wind, and physics-based MHD simulations with the CORHEL-CME framework to reconstruct the eruption from the low corona to 1 au.
AI.result: Simulations reproduce the observed CME morphology, asymmetric expansion, magnetic fields at both spacecraft, and Dst evolution; the main discrepancy is attributed to filament material omitted from the model. A right-handed flux rope in a complex environment dominated by a neighboring positive-polarity coronal hole experienced minimal interchange-reconnection erosion due to favorable polarity alignment, enabling rapid escape and preservation of the strong southward field. The prolonged recovery phase stemmed from interaction between the trailing CME and a following high-speed stream from the same coronal hole.
AI.conclusion: Storm intensity was primarily set by the coronal magnetic configuration, whereas storm duration was controlled by the ambient solar wind.

title: A new submillimeter Class I methanol maser at 345.903 GHz near the massive protostar S255IR NIRS3
comment: 6 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables
summary: We present results of further investigation of radio emission from the remarkable molecular core S255IR-SMA1 harboring a \(\sim\) 20 Msun young stellar object NIRS3 which exhibited a disk-mediated accretion burst in 2015. Our study is based on observations of this object with ALMA in Band 7 with the longest baselines, which provide an angular resolution of \(\sim\)15 mas. The obtained data reveal several spots in the bright and narrow methanol 16(1) \(-\) 15(2) A\(-\) line emission at 345.903 GHz. These spots are located close to H_2O masers, knots in the jet and arc-like structures seen in submillimeter continuum. At the same time, they are far away from the peaks of the Class II methanol maser spots. High brightness temperatures and small line widths of the 345.903 GHz line emission indicate that this emission has a maser nature. Association with the shock tracers tells that these masers belong to Class I methanol maser category. Non-LTE analysis of the physical parameters which lead to population inversion of 16(1) \(-\) 15(2) A\(-\) transition shows that some known rare Class I methanol maser transitions are also inverted under these conditions.

AI.tldr: ALMA Band 7 long-baseline observations of the S255IR-SMA1 core reveal narrow, high-brightness 345.903 GHz methanol masers (Class I), spatially linked to shock tracers and non-LTE models confirm population inversion of the 16(1)-15(2) A- transition.
AI.motivation: The massive young stellar object NIRS3 in S255IR-SMA1 underwent a disk-mediated accretion burst in 2015, making it an exceptional laboratory for studying maser emission and shock physics near a high-mass protostar; the nature and spatial distribution of the 345.903 GHz methanol line emission required clarification.
AI.method: ALMA Band 7 observations with the longest baselines (~15 mas angular resolution) toward S255IR-SMA1, mapping the 16(1)-15(2) A- methanol line at 345.903 GHz and comparing its positions with H2O masers, jet knots, submillimeter continuum arcs, and Class II methanol maser spots; supplemented by non-LTE radiative transfer analysis of the excitation conditions.
AI.result: Several compact 345.903 GHz emission spots are detected near H2O masers, jet knots, and arc-like submillimeter continuum structures, but far from Class II maser peaks. High brightness temperatures and narrow line widths indicate maser emission; association with shock tracers classifies them as Class I methanol masers. Non-LTE analysis shows the 16(1)-15(2) A- transition is inverted, and other rare Class I methanol maser transitions are also inverted under these conditions.
AI.conclusion: The 345.903 GHz line traces Class I methanol masers in shocked gas around the bursting massive YSO NIRS3, and the excitation analysis predicts additional rare Class I maser transitions, supporting a shock-driven maser scenario in this accretion-burst source.

title: Flashing with colours: Photometric indicators of an early interaction in type II supernovae
comment: 29 pages, 19 figures. Accepted for publication in A&A
summary: We present early-time optical photometry and spectroscopy for a sample 27 previously unpublished type II supernovae (SNe II) observed by the Precision Observations of Infant Supernova Explosions (POISE) collaboration, combined with a literature sample of 59 events to form a total sample of 86 objects. The resulting light curves comprise near-daily cadence, percent-level precision $uBgVri$ photometry. From spectra acquired within four days of the estimated explosion time, transient narrow emission lines of highly ionised elements, referred to as `flash features', can be identified. Based on the presence or absence of these lines, the SNe were categorised. We estimate key photometric properties, including rise times, peak absolute magnitude, and colour evolution. Our tests indicate that flash SNe are, on average, more luminous at the peak than their non-flash counterparts, which is consistent with previous studies. Interestingly, statistically significant differences were found in the rise times in the $B$ band, with flash SNe exhibiting a tail towards longer rise times. Flash SNe are generally bluer than non-flash events, with distinct colour distributions at 20 days post explosion, likely reflecting intrinsic differences rather than host-galaxy extinction. Colour-curve breaks within 30 days of explosion provide a clear separation between flash and non-flash SNe. The change in slopes across the break, combined with the absolute peak magnitude, yield a strong diagnostic of the flash-spectroscopic properties. This indicates that photometric observations alone may be used to identify SNe experiencing an interaction with dense circumstellar material, even in the absence of early-time spectroscopy.

AI.tldr: Early-time photometry and spectroscopy of 86 SNe II reveal that "flash" SNe (with high-ionization flash features) are more luminous, bluer, show longer B-band rise tails, and can be distinguished from non-flash events via color-curve breaks alone.
AI.motivation: Type II supernovae showing transient narrow high-ionization emission lines ("flash features") indicate interaction with dense circumstellar material, but systematic, high-cadence early-time characterization of these events is limited. The authors aim to establish robust photometric diagnostics that could identify such interacting SNe without requiring early spectroscopy.
